newsitem.title: UK: Dlr firm in late Europe, seen heading higher.
newsitem.headline: Dlr firm in late Europe, seen heading higher.

text.p: The dollar firmed against the mark in late European trade on Monday after recovering from an afternoon dip and was expected to continue to move up in a rally that has already pushed it to a 40-month high.

"The dollar is trending higher and there is clear evidence that people are eager to buy on dips. I think we could see a dollar/mark rate of 1.85 by year-end," said currency strategist Brian Martin at Barclays de Zeote Wedd.
Data earlier confirmed the U.S. economy was gearing up for further growth and while Martin did not see the FOMC hiking rates this week, he said a move up was clearly in the pipline.
"It's odds-on that they will raise rates in the latter part of the third quarter," he said.
Dollar-mark earlier brushed the 40-month high of 1.7465 and dealers agreed the market had higher levels fixed in its sights.

It slipped back from morning highs but a brief dip below 1.7400 met swift buying, said dealers. They blamed a European central bank seller of dollar-mark for triggering stop-losses at 1.7420 but expect the rally to continue.
"Dollar-mark is still a buy. There is interest on dips and it will probably test 1.7500 in the next day or two," said Nick Probert at Bank of America.

But Probert said that this target could prove a significant short-term barrier and cautioned that this would encourage dealers to set up speculative short positions ahead of the Federal Open Markets Committee that would fuel volatility.

The FOMC begins two days of sessions on Tuesday. With economists generally agreed that it would signal no change in rates, any action to the contrary would deliver an electric shock to the bid-side of dollar-mark.
"If the FOMC moves you won't see dollar/mark until 1.7800. Even if they don't move there is easily a couple more pfennigs' upside," said a senior dealer at one Japanese bank in London.

Mark woes and wider concern over the timing of a single European currency commanded the the market's attention all day, subduing Euroepan business in dollar-yen, with the market stuck in a narrow range between 114.70 and 114.18.
Elswhere, the Australian dollar stirred in late European trade, gaining close to one U.S. cent.
Nick Shamin, currency analyst at ANZ Investment, said there were "chunky" flows in the Aussie, notably in the Canada dollar cross as market players covered Aussie dollar short positions.
He said there was speculation the Reserve Bank of Australia might hold off for a while on cutting rates, at least to see what the U.S. Fed does at its policy meeting this week.
The Aussie dollar was quoted at US$0.7552/57, up from around $0.7460 earlier in Europe and from a Sydney close of $0.7453/58.
